messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 52
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Film Director
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 35

# Michael's Story

Michael sits in the director's chair on set, but he's not really there anymore. At fifty-two, he's spent thirty years behind the camera, building a reputation for meticulous attention to detail and innovative visual storytelling. His films have won festivals. He's worked with A-list actors. He knows every technical specification of every camera ever made. What he doesn't know is how to stop seeing the moment everything changed.

It was eighteen months ago, on a location shoot in Northern California. Michael was scouting a bridge for a crucial scene in his latest film—a dramatic sequence where the protagonist makes a life-altering decision. He'd walked out onto the structure alone, measuring angles and light, when the wooden railing gave way beneath him. He fell twenty-three feet onto rocks below, shattering his left femur, cracking three ribs, and rupturing his spleen. He remembers the sound—that specific crack of wood and bone. He remembers the weightlessness. He remembers the impact and then nothing until he woke up in a hospital bed with his partner Sarah holding his hand, her face streaked with tears.

The physical recovery took months. Surgery, physical therapy, the slow return to walking without a cane. But the physical healing was straightforward compared to everything else. Michael had started back to work six months ago, and on the surface, he was functioning. He showed up to set. He made creative decisions. He communicated with his crew. But something fundamental had fractured alongside his femur, and no amount of physical therapy could mend it.

Now, on set, Michael finds himself unable to stand near elevated platforms. During a recent shoot on a rooftop, he felt his chest tighten, his breathing shallow. He'd made an excuse about the light and moved the entire crew to a lower location, adding hours to the shooting schedule and thousands to the budget. His producer noticed but said nothing. Everyone knew about the accident.

The hypervigilance has woven itself into his daily life in ways both obvious and subtle. He inspects railings obsessively, running his hands along them, testing their stability. He avoids bridges entirely, taking circuitous routes through the city. When Sarah suggests they go to a rooftop bar—somewhere they used to love—he finds reasons to decline. She's stopped suggesting it.

Sleep has become a negotiation. Michael lies awake most nights, his mind replaying the fall in excruciating detail. Sometimes he dreams he's falling again, and he wakes gasping, his heart racing, his body drenched in sweat. Sarah has learned not to touch him when he wakes; the startle response is too intense. He's taken to sleeping in the guest room so his nightmares don't disturb her, though they both know it's really about his shame.

What troubles Michael most is the loss of his confidence. He's always trusted his instincts, his eye, his ability to see a story and know how to tell it. Now he second-guesses everything. When he's on set and something goes wrong—a light rig shifts, an actor misses a mark—his first thought is catastrophe. He can't shake the feeling that danger is imminent, that the world is fundamentally unsafe in ways he'd never considered before.

Sarah keeps telling him he should talk to someone. She's right, he knows. But Michael has spent his whole career being the one who sees, who interprets, who tells the story. The thought of sitting across from a therapist and admitting that he can't see his way through this—that the world has become too fragile, too unpredictable—feels like the final cut.
